claim: Loss of sensory hair cells leads to deafness and balance deficiencies.
source: Loss of sensory hair cells leads to deafness and balance deficiencies.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the consequences of hair cell loss.

claim: Zebrafish ear and lateral line hair cells regenerate from support cells.
source: In contrast to mammalian hair cells, zebrafish ear and lateral line hair cells regenerate from poorly characterized support cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field and is referenced in the introduction with citations.

claim: scRNA-Seq of lateral line organs uncovered five different support cell types, including quiescent and activated stem cells.
source: scRNA-Seq of lateral line organs uncovered five different support cell types, including quiescent and activated stem cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the scRNA-Seq data analysis presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 1 and related results.

claim: Ordering of support cells along a developmental trajectory identified self-renewing cells and genes required for hair cell differentiation.
source: Ordering of support cells along a developmental trajectory identified self-renewing cells and genes required for hair cell differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by the pseudotime analysis and trajectory inference performed on the scRNA-Seq data, as shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Fgf and Notch signaling inhibit proliferation of support cells in parallel by inhibiting Wnt signaling.
source: scRNA-Seq analyses of fgf3 mutants, in which hair cell regeneration is increased, demonstrates that Fgf and Notch signaling inhibit proliferation of support cells in parallel by inhibiting Wnt signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fgf3 mutant analysis, genetic epistasis experiments, and pathway manipulation studies shown in Figures 5-8.

claim: Non-mammalian vertebrates readily regenerate sensory hair cells during homeostasis and after injury.
source: Non-mammalian vertebrates readily regenerate sensory hair cells during homeostasis and after injury, whereas in mammals hair cell loss leads to permanent hearing and vestibular loss (Bermingham-McDonogh and Rubel, 2003; Brignull et al., 2009; Corwin and Cotanche, 1988; Cruz et al., 2015; Ryals and Rubel, 1988).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: In mammals hair cell loss leads to permanent hearing and vestibular loss.
source: Non-mammalian vertebrates readily regenerate sensory hair cells during homeostasis and after injury, whereas in mammals hair cell loss leads to permanent hearing and vestibular loss (Bermingham-McDonogh and Rubel, 2003; Brignull et al., 2009; Corwin and Cotanche, 1988; Cruz et al., 2015; Ryals and Rubel, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established research.

claim: The zebrafish lateral line system is a powerful in vivo model to study the cellular and molecular basis of hair cell regeneration.
source: We and others showed that the zebrafish lateral line system is a powerful in vivo model to study the cellular and molecular basis of hair cell regeneration (Kniss et al., 2016; Lush and Piotrowski, 2014b; Ma and Raible, 2009; Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015; Viader-Llargués et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work by the authors and others.

claim: Lateral line organs (neuromasts) contain approximately 60 cells, composed of central sensory hair cells surrounded by support cells and an outer ring of mantle cells.
source: The lateral line organs (neuromasts), distributed on the head and along the body contain approximately 60 cells, composed of central sensory hair cells surrounded by support cells and an outer ring of mantle cells (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by the description in the text and the schematic shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: The morphology and function of sensory hair cells are evolutionarily conserved from fish to mammals.
source: Importantly, the morphology and function of sensory hair cells are evolutionarily conserved from fish to mammals (Duncan and Fritzsch, 2012; Nicolson, 2005; Whitfield, 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mutations in genes causing deafness in humans also disrupt hair cells in the zebrafish lateral line.
source: For example, mutations in genes causing deafness in humans also disrupt hair cells in the zebrafish lateral line (Nicolson, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Notch signaling needs to be downregulated to activate Wnt-induced proliferation during hair cell regeneration in zebrafish.
source: In support of this hypothesis, our findings that Notch signaling needs to be downregulated to activate Wnt-induced proliferation during hair cell regeneration is also true in the mouse cochlea (Li et al., 2015b; Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work including the authors' own research.

claim: Notch signaling needs to be downregulated to activate Wnt-induced proliferation during hair cell regeneration in the mouse cochlea.
source: In support of this hypothesis, our findings that Notch signaling needs to be downregulated to activate Wnt-induced proliferation during hair cell regeneration is also true in the mouse cochlea (Li et al., 2015b; Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In zebrafish regeneration occurs via support cell proliferation and differentiation.
source: In zebrafish regeneration occurs via support cell proliferation and differentiation, and in chicken and amphibians hair cells regenerate from proliferating and transdifferentiating support cells (Balak et al., 1990; Bermingham-McDonogh and Rubel, 2003; Harris et al., 2003; Jones and Corwin, 1996; Lush and Piotrowski, 2014b; Ma et al., 2008; Wibowo et al., 2011; Williams and Holder, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: In chicken and amphibians hair cells regenerate from proliferating and transdifferentiating support cells.
source: In zebrafish regeneration occurs via support cell proliferation and differentiation, and in chicken and amphibians hair cells regenerate from proliferating and transdifferentiating support cells (Balak et al., 1990; Bermingham-McDonogh and Rubel, 2003; Harris et al., 2003; Jones and Corwin, 1996; Lush and Piotrowski, 2014b; Ma et al., 2008; Wibowo et al., 2011; Williams and Holder, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: There are two major support cell lineages: support cells that divide symmetrically to form two progenitor cells (amplifying divisions) and support cells that divide to form two hair cells (differentiating divisions).
source: Using time-lapse analyses and tracking of all dividing cells in regenerating neuromasts, coupled with cell fate analyses, we previously identified two major support cell lineages: 1) support cells that divide symmetrically to form two progenitor cells (amplifying divisions); and 2) support cells that divide to form two hair cells (differentiating divisions) (Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Amplifying divisions occur in the dorsal-ventral (D/V) poles and differentiating divisions occur in the center.
source: The two cell behaviors display a striking spatial compartmentalization. Amplifying divisions occur in the dorsal-ventral (D/V) poles and differentiating divisions occur in the center.
evidence: This is supported by prior experimental observations cited in the text and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Mantle cells surrounding the support cells only divide after severe injury to the neuromasts but rarely divide if only hair cells are killed.
source: Mantle cells surrounding the support cells only divide after severe injury to the neuromasts but rarely divide if only hair cells are killed.
evidence: This is based on prior experimental observations by the authors.

claim: There are at least four support cell types in a neuromast that likely play different functions in balancing progenitor maintenance with differentiation.
source: Thus, there are at least four support cell types in a neuromast that likely play different functions in balancing progenitor maintenance with differentiation to ensure the life-long ability to regenerate.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed cell behaviors and the scRNA-Seq analysis.

claim: Unsupervised clustering partitioned 1521 neuromast cells into 14 different clusters.
source: Unsupervised clustering partitioned 1521 neuromast cells into 14 different clusters (Butler et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct result from the scRNA-Seq data analysis.

claim: Seven major neuromast cell types were identified from the 14 clusters.
source: We combined some of the less well-defined clusters and identified seven major neuromast cell types (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is based on the scRNA-Seq analysis and shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Cluster 1 represents differentiated hair cells.
source: Based on marker gene expression, clusters 1, 2 and 4 encompass the hair cell lineage, with cluster one being differentiated hair cells, cluster two being young hair cells, and four representing proliferating hair cell progenitors (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is based on marker gene expression analysis from the scRNA-Seq data.

claim: Cluster 2 represents young hair cells.
source: Based on marker gene expression, clusters 1, 2 and 4 encompass the hair cell lineage, with cluster one being differentiated hair cells, cluster two being young hair cells, and four representing proliferating hair cell progenitors (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is based on marker gene expression analysis from the scRNA-Seq data.

claim: Cluster 4 represents proliferating hair cell progenitors.
source: Based on marker gene expression, clusters 1, 2 and 4 encompass the hair cell lineage, with cluster one being differentiated hair cells, cluster two being young hair cells, and four representing proliferating hair cell progenitors (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is based on marker gene expression analysis from the scRNA-Seq data.

claim: Clusters 3 and 10 represent amplifying support cells.
source: The other cycling cells belong to clusters 3 and 10, and because they fail to express hair cell lineage genes, they likely represent amplifying support cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the gene expression patterns in the scRNA-Seq data.

claim: Mature, differentiated hair cells are centrally and apically located in a neuromast.
source: Mature, differentiated hair cells are centrally and apically located in a neuromast (tekt3, Figure 1F,R,S; dark green).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1F, R, S.

claim: Young hair cells form a ring immediately above the mature hair cells and express atoh1b.
source: Immediately above the mature hair cells are young hair cells that form a ring and express atoh1b (cluster 2, Figure 1G,R,S).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1G, R, S.

claim: Delta ligands are only expressed in a subset of the young hair cells.
source: Figure 1H shows that delta ligands are only expressed in a subset of the young hair cells (light green).
evidence: This is shown by in situ hybridization data in Figure 1H.

claim: lfng and ebf3a mark the most basal, central support cells.
source: lfng and ebf3a mark the most basal, central support cells (Figure 1I,J,S,U; blue).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1I, J, S, U.

claim: lfng is expressed in support cells that are situated underneath hair cells in the mouse cochlea.
source: lfng is also expressed in support cells that are situated underneath hair cells in the mouse cochlea (Maass et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The central cell population in neuromasts expresses gata2a/b and slc1a3a/glasta, which are markers for hematopoietic and neural stem cells, respectively.
source: The central cell population in neuromasts expresses gata2a/b and slc1a3a/glasta, which are markers for hematopoietic and neural stem cells, respectively (Figure 3I; Supplementary file 6, Hewitt et al., 2016; Llorens-Bobadilla et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data and citations to prior research on these markers in other systems.

claim: A subset of central cells expresses stem cell-associated genes such as isl1 and fabp7a.
source: Within the central cell cluster, a subset of cells expresses other stem cell-associated genes, such as isl1 and fabp7a (clusters 7, 9; Figure 1K; Kim et al., 2016; Makarev and Gorivodsky, 2014; Morihiro et al., 2013; Shin et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1K and citations to prior research on these genes as stem cell markers.

claim: Members of the retinoic acid pathway, such as crabp2a, dhrs3a and rdh10a are restricted to clusters 7 and 9.
source: In addition, members of the retinoic acid pathway, such as crabp2a, dhrs3a and rdh10a are restricted to clusters 7 and 9 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on the scRNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Central cells only give rise to hair cells and do not self-renew.
source: Even though central cells express genes characteristic for stem cells in other systems, our lineage tracing experiments showed that they only give rise to hair cells and do not self-renew (Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior lineage tracing experiments by the authors.

claim: Cells in the D/V poles of neuromasts that express wnt2 are located immediately adjacent to the mantle cells and proliferate to generate more support cells that do not differentiate into hair cells.
source: Cells in the D/V poles of neuromasts that express wnt2 are located immediately adjacent to the mantle cells and proliferate to generate more support cells that do not differentiate into hair cells (see below; Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by prior experimental data cited from the authors' work.

claim: Mantle cells are the outermost cells in a neuromast and are marked by ovgp1 and sfrp1a.
source: The most distinct support cell population are the mantle cells represented in clusters 5 and 6 and marked by ovgp1 and sfrp1a (Figure 1M–N).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data and in situ hybridization shown in Figure 1M-N.

claim: Lineage tracing of mantle cells in medaka revealed that mantle cells give rise to support and hair cells and constitute long term stem cells.
source: Lineage tracing of mantle cells in medaka revealed that mantle cells give rise to support and hair cells and constitute long term stem cells (Seleit et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research in medaka.

claim: Mantle cells give rise to postembryonic neuromasts during development and restore neuromasts on regenerating tail tips.
source: In addition, they give rise to postembryonic neuromasts during development and restore neuromasts on regenerating tail tips (Dufourcq et al., 2006; Ghysen and Dambly-Chaudière, 2007; Jones and Corwin, 1993; Ledent, 2002; Wada et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Genes such as fndc7rs4, tfap2a, tcf7l2, hopx, cmah and alpl are expressed in a ring-like pattern in mantle cells, anterior-posterior (A/P) cells and polar cells.
source: We also identified a number of genes that are expressed in a ring-like pattern, such as fndc7rs4, tfap2a, tcf7l2, hopx, cmah and alpl (Figure 1O, data not shown). These genes are not restricted to any cluster but are expressed in mantle cells, anterior-posterior (A/P) cells and polar cells.
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data and in situ hybridization shown in Figure 1O.

claim: hopx, cmah and alpl are stem cell markers in different systems.
source: Interestingly, hopx, cmah and alpl are stem cell markers in different systems raising the possibility that they also mark stem cells in neuromasts (Fuchs, 2009; Takeda et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on these genes as stem cell markers.

claim: Cells in clusters 10, 3 and 4 express pcna (proliferating cell nuclear antigen) and stmn1a.
source: Cells in clusters 10, 3 and 4 express pcna (proliferating cell nuclear antigen), required for DNA replication and repair, as well as the mitotic spindle regulator stmn1a (Figures 1D, 2A and D; Supplementary file 4; Rubin and Atweh, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data shown in Figures 1D, 2A and D, and a citation to prior research on these genes.

claim: Genes that regulate early versus later phases of the cell cycle are expressed in complementary subsets of the pcna+ cells.
source: Genes that regulate early versus later phases of the cell cycle are expressed in complementary subsets of the pcna +cells (Figure 2B,C, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data shown in Figure 2B, C.

claim: Genes with GO terms DNA replication and DNA repair, such as mcm4, are expressed in cells closer to clusters 11 and 14.
source: Genes with the associated GO terms DNA replication and DNA repair, such as mcm4 are expressed in cells closer to clusters 11 and 14, whereas genes involved in chromosome segregation and mitosis are expressed in cells closer to the younger hair cells in the t-SNE plot (cdk1; Figure 2B,C and D).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data and GO term analysis shown in Figure 2B, C, D.

claim: Genes involved in chromosome segregation and mitosis are expressed in cells closer to the younger hair cells in the t-SNE plot.
source: Genes with the associated GO terms DNA replication and DNA repair, such as mcm4 are expressed in cells closer to clusters 11 and 14, whereas genes involved in chromosome segregation and mitosis are expressed in cells closer to the younger hair cells in the t-SNE plot (cdk1; Figure 2B,C and D).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data and GO term analysis shown in Figure 2B, C, D.

claim: Cluster 3 cells likely belong to the cluster of amplifying support cells adjacent to mantle cells that give rise to two undifferentiated daughter cells.
source: Thus, cluster 3 cells likely belong to the cluster of amplifying support cells adjacent to mantle cells that give rise to two undifferentiated daughter cells (Figure 2E–G; support cells, red), whereas cluster 4 cells are more central support cells that give rise to two daughters that differentiate into hair cells (Figure 2E–G; green cells, Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the scRNA-Seq data after regressing out cell cycle genes, and supported by prior lineage tracing data.

claim: Cluster 4 cells are more central support cells that give rise to two daughters that differentiate into hair cells.
source: Thus, cluster 3 cells likely belong to the cluster of amplifying support cells adjacent to mantle cells that give rise to two undifferentiated daughter cells (Figure 2E–G; support cells, red), whereas cluster 4 cells are more central support cells that give rise to two daughters that differentiate into hair cells (Figure 2E–G; green cells, Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the scRNA-Seq data after regressing out cell cycle genes, and supported by prior lineage tracing data.

claim: D/V poles possess more cells than the A/P poles.
source: D/V poles possess more cells than the A/P poles (Figure 2H), however, 6.5% of the D/V cells proliferate, whereas only 0–1% proliferate in the A/P poles (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by BrdU labeling data shown in Figure 2H, I.

claim: 6.5% of the D/V cells proliferate, whereas only 0–1% proliferate in the A/P poles.
source: D/V poles possess more cells than the A/P poles (Figure 2H), however, 6.5% of the D/V cells proliferate, whereas only 0–1% proliferate in the A/P poles (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by BrdU labeling data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Cells in the A/P poles and central cells beneath the hair cells are relatively quiescent during homeostasis.
source: Thus, cells in the A/P poles and central cells beneath the hair cells are relatively quiescent during homeostasis (Cruz et al., 2015; Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by BrdU labeling data and citations to prior research.

claim: The zona pellucida-like domain-containing protein one gene si:ch73-261i21.5 is expressed in quiescent cells in the A/P poles.
source: The expression of the zona pellucida-like domain-containing protein one gene si:ch73-261i21.5 in the A/P poles has a striking complementary expression pattern to the D/V maker wnt2 and is expressed in quiescent cells (Figure 2J–K).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2J-K.

claim: SoxB1 family member sox2, its target sox21a and sox3 are expressed in support and mantle cells but are downregulated in differentiated hair cells.
source: Node 17 shows that the SoxB1 family member sox2, its target sox21a and sox3 are expressed in support and mantle cells but are downregulated in differentiated hair cells (Figure 3D; Supplementary file 8, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3D and supplementary files.

claim: Mantle and all support cells constitute the prosensory domain in a lateral line neuromast.
source: Thus, mantle and all support cells constitute the prosensory domain in a lateral line neuromast.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression of SoxB1 genes in these cells, which characterize the prosensory domain in other species.

claim: Clusters 7, 9, 8, 14 and 4 comprise the differentiating hair cell lineage.
source: Clusters 7, 9, 8, 14 and 4 comprise the differentiating hair cell lineage, whereas clusters 5, 6, 12, 11, 10 and 3 encompass the amplifying lineage (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is inferred from gene expression patterns in the scRNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Clusters 5, 6, 12, 11, 10 and 3 encompass the amplifying lineage.
source: Clusters 7, 9, 8, 14 and 4 comprise the differentiating hair cell lineage, whereas clusters 5, 6, 12, 11, 10 and 3 encompass the amplifying lineage (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is inferred from gene expression patterns in the scRNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Lineage tracing experiments determined that central support cells give rise to hair cells.
source: Indeed, lineage tracing experiments determined that central support cells give rise to hair cells (Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015), whereas mantle cells give rise to support and hair cells if traced for several months and constitute long term stem cells (Seleit et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior lineage tracing experiments.

claim: Mantle cells give rise to support and hair cells if traced for several months and constitute long term stem cells.
source: Indeed, lineage tracing experiments determined that central support cells give rise to hair cells (Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015), whereas mantle cells give rise to support and hair cells if traced for several months and constitute long term stem cells (Seleit et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior lineage tracing experiments.

claim: Quiescent neural stem cells show low levels of ribosomal subunits and protein synthesis.
source: Quiescent neural stem cells show low levels of ribosomal subunits and protein synthesis (Llorens-Bobadilla et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Mantle cells and A/P cells express low levels of rpl and rps genes but these levels significantly increase in clusters 12 and 11 and the dividing cells in clusters 10 and 3.
source: Likewise, we observed mantle (clusters 5, 6) and A/P cells (cluster 13) expressing low levels of rpl (ribosomal protein-L) and rps (ribosomal protein small subunit) genes but these levels significantly increase in clusters 12 and 11 and the dividing cells in clusters 10 and 3 (Figure 3B' and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3B' and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The hair cell lineage and the central cells show little ribosome synthesis, which drastically increases in dividing hair cell progenitors.
source: Also, the hair cell lineage and the central cells (clusters 7, 8, 9 and 14) show little ribosome synthesis, which drastically increases in dividing hair cell progenitors (Figure 3C', Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3C' and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Central support and mantle cells resemble quiescent stem or progenitor cells based on their low ribosome synthesis levels.
source: The low ribosome synthesis levels suggest that central support and mantle cells resemble quiescent stem or progenitor cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the ribosome synthesis data and comparison to quiescent stem cells in other systems.

claim: When sost+ cells are displaced towards the center of the neuromasts, they downregulate sost and differentiate into hair cells.
source: However, when sost+ cells are displaced towards the center of the neuromasts, they downregulate sost and differentiate into hair cells (lineage from clusters 11/14 to 4, green arrow in Figure 3B and G).
evidence: This is inferred from the scRNA-Seq data and supported by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 3B and G.

claim: The differentiating lineage is marked by atoh1a which specifies hair cells together with the downstream delta ligands.
source: The differentiating lineage is marked by atoh1a which specifies hair cells together with the downstream delta ligands (Figures 3H and 4A).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data shown in Figures 3H and 4A.

claim: atoh1a is expressed in non-cycling (clusters 7, 8, 9 and 14) and cycling hair cell progenitors (cluster 4), as well as young hair cells (cluster 2).
source: atoh1a is expressed in non-cycling (clusters 7, 8, 9 and 14) and cycling hair cell progenitors (cluster 4), as well as young hair cells (cluster 2).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data.

claim: Central cells are marked by progenitor markers slc1a3a/glasta, lfng, ebf3a, gata2b and prox1a.
source: These cells belong to a subset of central support cells that are marked by progenitor markers slc1a3a/glasta, lfng, ebf3a, gata2b and prox1a (Figure 1I–J and Figure 3I–K, Supplementary file 8, nodes 26, 22 and 7).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data shown in Figures 1I-J and 3I-K.

claim: Time lapse analyses of regenerating neuromasts in a prox1a reporter line show that central cells downregulate prox1a as they divide, while turning on the hair cell marker pou4f3:gfp.
source: Indeed, time lapse analyses of regenerating neuromasts in a prox1a reporter line show that central cells downregulate prox1a as they divide, while turning on the hair cell marker pou4f3:gfp (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3-video 1), as described for the mouse cochlea (Bermingham-McDonogh et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and a citation to prior research in the mouse cochlea.

claim: Central cells (clusters 7, 9, 8, 14 and 4) contain or represent hair cell progenitors.
source: We conclude that central cells (clusters 7, 9, 8,14 and 4) contain or represent hair cell progenitors.
evidence: This is inferred from the gene expression patterns and time-lapse data.

claim: Hair cells are subdivided into younger hair cells (cluster 2) and mature hair cells (cluster 1) based on differential gene expression.
source: However, hair cells are subdivided into younger hair cells (cluster 2) and mature hair cells based on differential gene expression (cluster 1; Supplementary file 3, nodes 1 and 2), but the younger hair cells in cluster two possess cilia and can be killed with neomycin (Figure 1R–S; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data and experimental observations shown in Figure 1R-S and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Younger hair cells in cluster 2 possess cilia and can be killed with neomycin.
source: However, hair cells are subdivided into younger hair cells (cluster 2) and mature hair cells based on differential gene expression (cluster 1; Supplementary file 3, nodes 1 and 2), but the younger hair cells in cluster two possess cilia and can be killed with neomycin (Figure 1R–S; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1R-S and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: fndc7a labels support cells and the more apically located young and mature hair cells are unlabeled.
source: For example, in situ hybridization with fndc7a shows that it labels support cells as in the mouse and that the more apically located young and mature hair cells are unlabeled (Figure 4K; Maass et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4K and a citation to prior research in the mouse.

claim: A Tg(NFκB:EGFP) reporter line shows that the NFκB pathway is expressed in support cells but that hair cells are GFP-negative.
source: Likewise, a Tg(NFκB:EGFP) reporter line shows that the NFκB pathway that regulates proliferation and self-renewal in other systems is expressed in support cells but that hair cells are GFP-negative (Figure 4L–N; Kanther et al., 2011; Rinkenbaugh and Baldwin, 2016; Zakaria et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data from the reporter line shown in Figure 4L-N and citations to prior research on NFκB.

claim: Genes associated with regulation of transcription, translation, protein folding, cell cycle and Wnt signaling are downregulated in clusters 1 and 2.
source: A GO term analysis reveals that genes associated with regulation of transcription, translation, protein folding, cell cycle and Wnt signaling are downregulated in clusters 1 and 2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by GO term analysis of the scRNA-Seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Genes associated with translation, regulation of cell cycle and Notch signaling (dla, dlb, dlc, dld) are downregulated as hair cells develop from young to mature hair cells.
source: Another group of genes is downregulated as hair cells develop from young to mature hair cells (Figure 4O, Supplementary file 8, node 2 and 24). These downregulated genes are associated with the GO terms translation, regulation of cell cycle and Notch signaling (dla, dlb, dlc, dld).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data and GO term analysis shown in Figure 4O and supplementary files.

claim: Fgf pathway genes are downregulated 1 hr after hair cell death.
source: Our previous bulk RNA-Seq analysis of regenerating neuromasts revealed that Fgf pathway genes are downregulated 1 hr after hair cell death ((Jiang et al., 2014; Figure 5A–H') suggesting that the downregulation of Fgf signaling could be involved in triggering regeneration, as was shown for Notch signaling (Ma et al., 2008; Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by prior bulk RNA-Seq data and in situ hybridization shown in Figure 5A-H', and citations to prior research.

claim: Hair cell regeneration is enhanced in fgf3 mutant larvae.
source: Indeed, hair cell regeneration is enhanced in fgf3 mutant larvae and even during homeostasis the total cell number per neuromast is increased (Figure 5I–L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5I-L.

claim: During homeostasis the total cell number per neuromast is increased in fgf3 mutant larvae.
source: Indeed, hair cell regeneration is enhanced in fgf3 mutant larvae and even during homeostasis the total cell number per neuromast is increased (Figure 5I–L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5I-L.

claim: fgf3 is expressed exclusively in central support cells (clusters 7, 8, 9) and is downregulated in response to death of the overlying hair cells.
source: The scRNA-Seq analysis of homeostatic neuromasts shows that ligand and receptor expression is complex, and that Fgf signaling is not active in young or mature hair cells (Figure 5M; clusters 2, 1). fgf3 is expressed exclusively in central support cells (clusters 7, 8, 9) and is downregulated in response to death of the overlying hair cells (Figure 5A').
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data shown in Figure 5M and in situ hybridization shown in Figure 5A'.

claim: fgf3 and prox1a are co-expressed in central support cells.
source: We generated a fgf3 knock-in line that recapitulates fgf3 expression (Figure 5N–O, Figure 5-video 1) and a cross with a prox1a reporter line shows that fgf3 and prox1a are co-expressed, as predicted by the scRNA-Seq data (Figure 5P–Q).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data from the fgf3 knock-in and prox1a reporter lines shown in Figure 5P-Q.

claim: During both homeostasis and regeneration, proliferation is significantly increased in fgf3-/- neuromasts.
source: To understand the cellular basis of the increased regeneration response, we performed BrdU analyses of homeostatic and regenerating fgf3-deficient neuromasts. During both homeostasis and regeneration, proliferation is significantly increased in fgf3-/- neuromasts (Figure 6A–F).
evidence: This is supported by BrdU labeling data shown in Figure 6A-F.

claim: Downregulation of Fgf signaling by expression of dn:fgfr1a during homeostasis increases proliferation.
source: Downregulation of Fgf signaling by expression of dn:fgfr1a during homeostasis also increases proliferation and neuromasts are significantly bigger in fgfr1a/fgfr2 double mutants, similarly to fgf3-/- (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Figure 6G–L, Figure 5L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6G-L.

claim: Neuromasts are significantly bigger in fgfr1a/fgfr2 double mutants, similarly to fgf3-/-.
source: Downregulation of Fgf signaling by expression of dn:fgfr1a during homeostasis also increases proliferation and neuromasts are significantly bigger in fgfr1a/fgfr2 double mutants, similarly to fgf3-/- (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Figure 6G–L, Figure 5L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G-L and Figure 5L.

claim: fgf3 likely signals via fgfr1a and fgfr2 receptors.
source: Therefore, fgf3 likely signals via fgfr1a and fgfr2 receptors.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic similarity between fgf3 mutants and fgfr1a/fgfr2 double mutants.

claim: In fgf3-/- homeostatic and regenerating neuromasts amplifying divisions are not restricted to the D/V poles.
source: The BrdU plots and the rose diagrams show that in fgf3-/- homeostatic and regenerating neuromasts amplifying divisions are not restricted to the D/V poles (Figure 6B–B' and D–D').
evidence: This is supported by BrdU labeling data shown in Figure 6B-B' and D-D'.

claim: The pattern of proliferating cells in fgf3-/- looks almost identical to the ones observed after upregulation of Wnt signaling.
source: This pattern of proliferating cells looks almost identical to the ones observed after upregulation of Wnt signaling (Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred by comparing the current data to prior experimental observations.

claim: The variance between the fgf3 mutant and sibling scRNA-Seq datasets is small as the two datasets intermingle in the t-SNE plot.
source: A t-SNE plot in which we plotted mutant and sibling datasets together demonstrates that the variance between the two datasets is small as the two datasets intermingle (Figure 7A, sibling blue, mutant red).
evidence: This is shown by the integrated t-SNE plot in Figure 7A.

claim: Mutant cells contribute to each cluster and therefore no major cell type is missing in fgf3-/-.
source: The plot also shows that mutant cells contribute to each cluster and that therefore no major cell type is missing in fgf3-/- (Figures 7A–B and 1D).
evidence: This is shown by the integrated t-SNE plot in Figures 7A-B.

claim: Some of the D/V polar genes, such as sost and adcyap1b are downregulated in fgf3 mutants.
source: We were particularly interested in genes that regulate the Wnt pathway and/or proliferation and identified that some of the D/V polar genes, such as sost and adcyap1b are downregulated in the mutants (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: sost is downregulated in fgf3-/- and dn:fgfr1 larvae.
source: We validated the downregulation of Wnt inhibitor sost by in situ hybridization in fgf3-/- and dn:fgfr1 larvae (Figure 7D–E').
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7D-E'.

claim: sost is downregulated 1 hr after hair cell death in wild type larvae.
source: Interestingly, sost is also downregulated 1 hr after hair cell death in wild type larvae, suggesting that the downregulation of Fgf signaling after neomycin could also be responsible for the downregulation of the Wnt inhibitor sost (Figure 7F–F').
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7F-F'.

claim: The Wnt target gene wnt10a is upregulated in fgf3 mutants.
source: Also, the Wnt target gene wnt10a is upregulated, illustrating that Wnt signaling is increased in fgf3 mutants (Figure 7G–G', Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7G-G' and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: hs:dkk1 significantly inhibits proliferation in siblings and also reduces proliferation and hair cell numbers in fgf3-/-.
source: To interrogate if the increase in proliferation in Fgf pathway mutants is due to the upregulation of Wnt signaling, we abrogated Wnt signaling in fgf3-/- by crossing them with hs:dkk1 fish. hs:dkk1 significantly inhibits proliferation in siblings and it also reduces proliferation and hair cell numbers in fgf3-/- (Figure 8A–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A-F.

claim: In homeostatic neuromasts fgf3 inhibits proliferation by inhibiting Wnt signaling, possibly via sost.
source: Therefore, in homeostatic neuromasts fgf3 inhibits proliferation by inhibiting Wnt signaling, possibly via sost.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that Wnt inhibition rescues the fgf3 mutant phenotype and that sost is downregulated in fgf3 mutants.

claim: Fgf signaling does not act upstream of Notch signaling, as Notch pathway members are not affected by in situ hybridization in fgf3-/-.
source: Fgf signaling does not act upstream of Notch signaling, as Notch pathway members are not affected by in situ hybridization in fgf3-/- (Figure 8G–K', Figure 9).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 8G-K'.

claim: fgf3 is slightly downregulated after Notch signaling inhibition with a γ-secretase inhibitor.
source: fgf3 on the other hand, is slightly downregulated after Notch signaling inhibition with a γ-secretase inhibitor (Figure 8M') while fgf10a and fgfr1a are not affected (Figure 8O–P').
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 8M' and O-P'.

claim: Notch signaling may play some minor role in inducing/maintaining fgf3 expression.
source: It is therefore possible that Notch signaling plays some minor role in inducing/maintaining fgf3 expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that fgf3 is slightly downregulated after Notch inhibition.

claim: Notch signaling does not inhibit Wnt signaling via the upregulation of Fgf3 signaling.
source: However, Notch signaling does not inhibit Wnt signaling via the upregulation of Fgf3 signaling, as shown by experiments in which we constitutively activated Notch signaling in fgf3-/- by expressing the Notch intracellular domain NICD.
evidence: This is supported by epistasis experiments shown in Figure 8Q-V.

claim: Activation of NICD in siblings during regeneration strongly inhibits proliferation and hair cell production.
source: Activation of NICD in siblings during regeneration strongly inhibits proliferation and hair cell production (Figure 8Q,R,U,V, Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015; Wibowo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8Q, R, U, V and citations to prior research.

claim: Activation of NICD in fgf3-/- strongly inhibits proliferation and hair cell numbers.
source: Activation of NICD in fgf3-/- also strongly inhibits proliferation and hair cell numbers demonstrating that Notch signaling does not require Fgf to inhibit Wnt signaling (Figure 8S–V).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8S-V.

claim: Notch and Fgf signaling largely act in parallel to inhibit Wnt signaling, with a small amount of proliferation being inhibited by Notch via the upregulation of Fgf signaling.
source: We conclude from these data that Notch and Fgf signaling largely act in parallel to inhibit Wnt signaling, with a small amount of proliferation being inhibited by Notch via the upregulation of Fgf signaling (Figure 9).
evidence: This is inferred from the epistasis experiments and shown in the model in Figure 9.

claim: Notch and Fgf need both to be independently and transiently downregulated for efficient hair cell regeneration.
source: Thus Notch and Fgf need both to be independently and transiently downregulated for efficient hair cell regeneration.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that both pathways inhibit proliferation in parallel.

claim: The amplifying and hair cell lineages are not predetermined, but rather the location of cells within the neuromast and the signals they are exposed to determine their fate.
source: This hypothesis is supported by time lapse movies of amplifying support cells during homeostasis and regeneration (Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015). Our finding shows that the amplifying and hair cell lineages are not predetermined, but rather that the location of cells within the neuromast and the signals they are exposed to determine their fate.
evidence: This is inferred from the PAGA graph showing connections between amplifying and differentiating cells, and supported by time-lapse data.

claim: Lateral line neuromasts possess active and quiescent stem cells.
source: Based on cell behavior and gene expression studies we postulate that lateral line neuromasts possess active and quiescent stem cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the cell behavior, proliferation patterns, and gene expression data.

claim: Amplifying cells in the D/V poles represent active stem cells.
source: Because amplifying support cells in the D/V poles self-renew continuously and only differentiate if displaced into the center, we postulate that amplifying cells represent active stem cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed cell behaviors and proliferation patterns.

claim: Cells in the A/P compartment are relatively quiescent during homeostasis and regeneration and may represent a quiescent stem cell population.
source: The first population are cells in the A/P compartment that are relatively quiescent during homeostasis and regeneration (Figure 2H, (Cruz et al., 2015; Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015). These cells start to proliferate after manipulations of the Fgf, Notch or Wnt pathways (Figure 6D, Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from proliferation data and pathway manipulation experiments.

claim: Mantle cells are quiescent, long term stem cells that give rise to hair cells in long term lineage analyses but do not respond to acute neomycin-induced hair cell death.
source: The second quiescent, long term stem cell population are the mantle cells that give rise to hair cells in long term lineage analyses but that do not respond to acute neomycin-induced hair cell death (Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015; Seleit et al., 2017; Viader-Llargués et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior lineage tracing studies.

claim: Support cells give rise to mantle cells when mantle cells are ablated.
source: Support cells also give rise to mantle cells when mantle cells are ablated (Viader-Llargués et al., 2018) arguing that active and quiescent stem cells can convert back and forth as shown in other systems (Clevers and Watt, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Quiescent stem cells in various systems are distinguished by their low level of protein synthesis and transcription.
source: Quiescent stem cells in hematopoiesis, the brain, skeletal muscle, hair follicle and Drosophila germline stem cells are also distinguished by their low level of protein synthesis and transcription (Blanco et al., 2016; Llorens-Bobadilla et al., 2015; Sanchez et al., 2016; Signer et al., 2014; Zismanov et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: A characteristic of stem cell activation is the upregulation of protein synthesis and associated factors, such as ribosomal proteins.
source: A characteristic of stem cell activation is consequently the upregulation of protein synthesis and associated factors, such as ribosomal proteins (Baser et al., 2017; Signer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Support cells share gene expression profiles with stem cells in the CNS, heart, intestine or hair follicles.
source: The notion that some support cells constitute stem cells is also supported by the finding that their gene expression profiles share a number of genes with stem cells in the CNS, heart, intestine or hair follicles.
evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data and comparisons to stem cell markers in other systems.

claim: Neural stem cells in the subventricular zone of the CNS and radial glial cells are characterized by glutamate aspartate transporter (GLAST) and Prominin-1 (CD133) expression.
source: For example, neural stem cells in the subventricular zone of the CNS and radial glial cells are characterized by glutamate aspartate transporter (GLAST) and Prominin-1 (also known as CD133) expression (Llorens-Bobadilla et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In neuromasts, slc1a3a/glasta and prominin1a are expressed strongly in central and A/P support cells and prominin1b is specifically enriched in A/P cells.
source: In neuromasts, slc1a3a/glasta and prominin1a are expressed strongly in central and A/P support cells and prominin1b is specifically enriched in A/P cells.
evidence: This is supported by the scRNA-Seq data.

claim: hopx and alpl are associated with intestinal, hair follicle and neural stem cells and are strongly expressed in mantle, A/P, and amplifying cells adjacent to mantle cells in neuromasts.
source: Likewise, genes associated with intestinal, hair follicle and neural stem cells (NSCs), such hopx and alpl are strongly expressed in mantle, A/P, and amplifying cells adjacent to mantle cells, but are downregulated in central support cells, forming a ring of expression similarly to fndc7rs4 (Figure 1O and Figure 3G, Li et al., 2015a; Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data and citations to prior research on these genes as stem cell markers.

claim: fabp7/Blbp labels glioma stem cells, radial glia cells, and neural stem cells.
source: Genes specifically expressed in central support cells beneath the hair cells likewise express genes that label stem cells in other organs, such as fabp7/Blbp, which labels glioma stem cells, radial glia cells, NSCs, (Kim et al., 2016; Morihiro et al., 2013) and isl1 that is expressed in quiescent intestinal stem cells and stem cells in the heart (Makarev and Gorivodsky, 2014; Shin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: isl1 is expressed in quiescent intestinal stem cells and stem cells in the heart.
source: Genes specifically expressed in central support cells beneath the hair cells likewise express genes that label stem cells in other organs, such as fabp7/Blbp, which labels glioma stem cells, radial glia cells, NSCs, (Kim et al., 2016; Morihiro et al., 2013) and isl1 that is expressed in quiescent intestinal stem cells and stem cells in the heart (Makarev and Gorivodsky, 2014; Shin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In lateral line neuromasts central cells only give rise to hair cells and are therefore not considered stem cells.
source: However, in lateral line neuromasts central cells only give rise to hair cells and we therefore do not consider them to be stem cells.
evidence: This is based on prior lineage tracing experiments.

claim: Wnt signaling induces and is required for support cell proliferation in neuromasts.
source: Wnt signaling induces and is required for support cell proliferation in neuromasts (Head et al., 2013; Jacques et al., 2014; Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015; Wada and Kawakami, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: In fgf3-/- Wnt signaling is upregulated causing cells to proliferate.
source: In fgf3-/- Wnt signaling is upregulated causing cells to proliferate (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Of the neuromast-expressed secreted Wnt inhibitors sfrp1a, dkk2, sost and sostdc1b, only sost is downregulated in fgf3-/-.
source: We found that of the neuromast-expressed secreted Wnt inhibitors sfrp1a, dkk2, sost and sostdc1b, only sost is downregulated in fgf3-/- (Figure 7D', data not shown, Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015; Wada et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq and in situ hybridization data.

claim: Wnt signaling induces proliferation in mammalian hair cell progenitors.
source: As Wnt signaling also induces proliferation in mammalian hair cell progenitors (Chai et al., 2012; Jacques et al., 2012; Jan et al., 2013; Samarajeewa et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2012) a role for Sost paralogs in this system should be tested.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Sost is not, or only lowly expressed in the mammalian ear sensory epithelia, whereas Sostdc1 is robustly expressed.
source: According to several data bases, Sost is not, or only lowly expressed in the mammalian ear sensory epithelia, whereas Sostdc1 is robustly expressed.
evidence: This is based on information from databases.

claim: Fgf signaling could inhibit proliferation by regulating other receptor tyrosine kinase activities, for example via inhibition of EGFR by Sprouty2.
source: Fgf signaling could also inhibit proliferation by regulating other receptor tyrosine kinase activities, for example via inhibition of EGFR by Sprouty2 (Balasooriya et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculation based on a citation to prior research.

claim: sprouty2 is downregulated in fgf3-/- after hair cell death.
source: sprouty2 is also down regulated in fgf3-/- after hair cell death and could perform a similar inhibitory function in homeostatic neuromasts (Supplementary file 14).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-Seq data in Supplementary file 14.

claim: Fgf signaling inhibits proliferation in the regenerating utricle and the basilar papilla of chicken.
source: Fgf signaling also inhibits proliferation in the regenerating utricle and the basilar papilla of chicken (Jiang et al., 2018; Ku et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Addition of Fgf2 or Fgf20 to auditory or vestibular cultures inhibits support cell proliferation.
source: Likewise, addition of Fgf2 or Fgf20 to auditory or vestibular cultures inhibits support cell proliferation (Ku et al., 2014; Oesterle et al., 2000), suggesting that the inhibitory effect of Fgf signaling on progenitor proliferation is evolutionary conserved in species that can regenerate their sensory hair cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The inhibitory effect of Fgf signaling on progenitor proliferation is evolutionary conserved in species that can regenerate their sensory hair cells.
source: Likewise, addition of Fgf2 or Fgf20 to auditory or vestibular cultures inhibits support cell proliferation (Ku et al., 2014; Oesterle et al., 2000), suggesting that the inhibitory effect of Fgf signaling on progenitor proliferation is evolutionary conserved in species that can regenerate their sensory hair cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the data in zebrafish and citations to prior research in other species.

claim: It is possible that fgf3 acts to maintain hair cell progenitors in an undifferentiated, non-sensory state as has been observed in the developing zebrafish ear.
source: While our data suggest that the main role of fgf3 in mature neuromasts is in regulating proliferation, it is also possible that fgf3 acts to maintain hair cell progenitors in an undifferentiated, non-sensory state as has been observed in the developing zebrafish ear (Maier and Whitfield, 2014).
evidence: This is speculation based on a citation to prior research.

claim: In the mouse cochlea loss of Fgfr3 results in increased hair cells at the expense of support cells.
source: Likewise, in the mouse cochlea loss of Fgfr3 results in increased hair cells at the expense of support cells (Hayashi et al., 2007; Puligilla et al., 2007), while activating mutations in Fgfr3 or loss of function mutation in the Fgfr inhibitor Spry2 lead to transformation of one support cell type into another (Mansour et al., 2013; Mansour et al., 2009; Shim et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Activating mutations in Fgfr3 or loss of function mutation in the Fgfr inhibitor Spry2 lead to transformation of one support cell type into another in the mouse cochlea.
source: Likewise, in the mouse cochlea loss of Fgfr3 results in increased hair cells at the expense of support cells (Hayashi et al., 2007; Puligilla et al., 2007), while activating mutations in Fgfr3 or loss of function mutation in the Fgfr inhibitor Spry2 lead to transformation of one support cell type into another (Mansour et al., 2013; Mansour et al., 2009; Shim et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A possible inhibitory effect of fgf3 on hair cell fate has to be rather subtle, as only a limited increase in hair cell numbers is observed.
source: However, a possible inhibitory effect of fgf3 on hair cell fate has to be rather subtle, as we only observe a limited increase in hair cell numbers, and our scRNA-Seq analyses did not reveal any obvious candidates that might regulate cell fate in a Fgf-dependent fashion.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations and scRNA-Seq data.

claim: Notch signaling is immediately downregulated after hair cell death causing cell proliferation.
source: Just like Fgf, Notch signaling is immediately downregulated after hair cell death causing cell proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: During homeostasis both Fgf and Notch pathways inhibit proliferation through negative regulation of Wnt activity.
source: During homeostasis both pathways inhibit proliferation through negative regulation of Wnt activity (Ma et al., 2008; Romero-Carvajal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In mammals a short inhibition of Notch and/or Fgf pathways is more likely to result in functional regeneration than prolonged treatments.
source: As such, in mammals a short inhibition of one or both of these pathways is more likely to result in functional regeneration than prolonged treatments.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that both pathways are reactivated before regeneration is complete.
